content: The Association of State and Territorial Health Officials (ASTHO) conducted a comprehensive survey of state health department personnel to evaluate programs, policies, and public health systems aimed at preventing and controlling tobacco use. This survey assessed various components, including budgets, planning, coalitions, surveillance systems, smoking cessation programs, educational activities, legislative actions, and health department policies. The findings revealed significant variability among states in the strength and coverage of their tobacco prevention and control programs. The ASTHO survey data can be utilized to plan and evaluate state health department programs as part of broader efforts to prevent chronic diseases associated with tobacco use. Outcomes of state activities can be assessed through surveys such as the CDC's Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) and the Current Population Survey (CPS) conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau. Future surveys may also contribute to evaluating the effectiveness of upcoming initiatives. In October 1989, ASTHO conducted this survey to assess progress among states in public health practices related to tobacco use prevention and control. The survey also aimed to incentivize states to develop and implement tobacco control efforts. It covered multiple components of effective state programs targeting specific populations. Additional data sources were used to supplement or validate state information on tobacco control activities. In the fall of 1989, ASTHO established a network of health professionals to facilitate communication between the federal government and state health departments on tobacco prevention and control issues. These professionals served as key contacts for information exchange and as respondents to the ASTHO survey. The survey was divided into ten major sections: background information on tobacco and tobacco control, adult tobacco-use surveillance, adolescent tobacco-use surveillance, data reporting and analysis on tobacco-related disease impact, regulatory activities, coalitions against tobacco use, special populations, community education activities, economic incentives and deterrents, and educational institutions. ASTHO contacts collaborated with state education departments to address questions about tobacco control activities in schools, assessing progress toward smoke-free schools and the extent of anti-tobacco education. Central data sources supplemented survey results in areas such as legislative activities, taxation, and school-related data. Legislative information was drawn from sources like the Tobacco-Free America Project and the National Institutes of Health. State-specific taxation data were provided by the Tobacco Institute. School-related data were supplemented by the 1990 World Almanac. Previously tabulated data were reviewed and updated by the ASTHO network in December 1990. ASTHO distributed the survey to all 50 states and the District of Columbia, treating the latter as a state for summary data purposes. Supplemental information was occasionally obtained via telephone. Responses were analyzed using software tools like True Epistat and dBase IV. The response rate for both the main and educational sections of the survey was 100%. As of October 1990, 12 states had developed standalone plans for tobacco use prevention and control, while 22 states included such plans within broader chronic disease control strategies. These plans addressed high-risk populations, healthcare, smoking cessation, workplace policies, and other areas. The average state budget for tobacco-related health activities, excluding California, was $70,917, with 27 states reporting no funds allocated. California allocated $151 million, funded by a portion of its cigarette excise tax. Six other states also earmarked excise tax revenues for public health activities. Additional funding sources, including grants and cooperative agreements, averaged $54,230 per state. The CDC's BRFSS, a telephone-based system, collected annual data on tobacco use and other health-related behaviors among adults aged 18 and older. In 1990, 46 states participated in the BRFSS. Twenty-one states collected adult smoking prevalence data from non-BRFSS sources, with 20 of these states focusing on specific target populations, such as racial and ethnic minorities, individuals with low socioeconomic status, and women of reproductive age. No national system existed for monitoring state-specific adolescent tobacco use. However, the CDC developed the Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS) to collect comparable school-based data. By January 1990, three states had participated in the YRBS, with 19 additional states joining by the end of the year. States also collected data on tobacco experimentation, current use, age of initiation, and smokeless tobacco use. Twenty-six states had information on experimentation, 32 on prevalence, 19 on age of initiation, and 25 on smokeless tobacco use. All 51 state health departments used the Smoking-Attributable Mortality, Morbidity, and Economic Costs (SAMMEC) software to obtain data on smoking-related deaths and economic costs. Five states required smoking history on death certificates, four reported data on smoking-attributable hospital discharges, and eight had information on state-funded medical care costs related to smoking. Maternal smoking history was recorded on birth certificates in 33 states. In 1989, 45 states had laws restricting smoking in public places, with 38 extending these restrictions to public-sector workplaces and 17 to private-sector workplaces. Local smoking ordinances covered various public settings, including restaurants, elevators, hotels, libraries, and public transit. A total of 490 local ordinances restricted or prohibited smoking in public places. All state health departments, except those in North Carolina and Virginia, had written policies on smoking in state health department buildings in 1989. Twenty-four states completely banned smoking in these facilities, while 31 permitted the sale of tobacco products within health department buildings. As of October 1990, 46 states prohibited the sale of tobacco products to minors, with minimum purchase ages ranging from 16 to 19 years. Nine states restricted the placement of vending machines containing tobacco products, with Colorado banning smokeless tobacco sales in vending machines and Utah banning all tobacco product sales in vending machines. Twenty-two states required state-issued retail tobacco licenses for vendors, with fees ranging from $0 to $250. Two states, Massachusetts and Utah, restricted tobacco advertising on state property. Local policies in six states restricted advertising on local government property, such as buses and sports facilities. By October 1990, all 50 states had tobacco-related coalitions or working groups representing health professionals, community members, legislative advocates, and educational groups. These coalitions engaged in public education, legislative efforts, professional education, planning, and research. The average funding for coalitions, excluding California, was $5,536. Forty states had programs targeting high-risk populations, including adolescents, women of reproductive age, and racial and ethnic minorities. Thirty-three states offered smoking cessation programs, and 26 collected behavioral data on these populations. Twenty-two state health departments produced public service announcements to prevent tobacco use, while 45 used federally produced announcements. Thirty-two states initiated public information campaigns using various media forms within the last two years. Thirty-five states offered smoking cessation programs to state health employees, and 26 extended these programs to community members. Colorado, Kansas, and Washington provided health benefits packages with differential rates for smokers and non-smokers among state government employees. Fourteen states reported third-party payers offering differential rates, and seven states offered reimbursement for tobacco addiction treatment. State tobacco excise taxes ranged from 2 cents per pack in North Carolina to 41 cents per pack in Texas, with an average of 23 cents per pack. Lower tax rates were primarily found in tobacco-producing states. Thirty-nine states had laws restricting tobacco use in schools, with 27 banning smoking for students and eight banning it for both students and staff. Sixteen states reported formal policies on tobacco use in schools. Only two states, Ohio and Nevada, provided information on private schools. Data indicated that 15,323 school districts existed in the U.S., with varying levels of smoking bans and tobacco-use prevention education. The 1989 ASTHO survey provided baseline data on state activities related to tobacco use prevention and control. States varied widely in their approaches, with some implementing extensive programs and others having limited resources. Linking survey data with state-specific smoking prevalence and cessation data can help assess the outcomes of recent activities. Future surveys may measure progress toward national health objectives outlined in Healthy People 2000, which includes 16 tobacco-related goals. These surveys are essential for evaluating public health efforts to prevent and control tobacco use.
